title: Set a small part on a surface grinder's magnetic chuck and block it in
instruction: Set the blue steel part flat on the magnetic chuck for grinding: lengthwise against the rail along the chuck's left edge, straddling one of the brass lines. Then block it in: put a blocking piece against each end of the part, using only pieces lower than the part so the grinding wheel passes over them. Let go of everything when done.
context: Surface grinding is everyday machine-shop work (O*NET 51-4041 Machinists; 51-4033 Grinding, Lapping, Polishing and Buffing Machine Tool Setters, Operators and Tenders). A surface grinder holds the work on a magnetic chuck whose face is steel pole pieces separated by non-magnetic brass lines: a part is held only where it bridges a brass line from one pole to the next, so a small part sitting on a single pole is barely held. Small parts are set against the chuck's back rail (here along its left edge) and blocked in: steel pieces butted against their ends stop the wheel pushing them along the table. The blocking must be lower than the part so the wheel passes over it; a piece taller than the part is struck by the wheel. Nothing is energised or turning here: the end state is what a setter checks before starting the table, and picking blocking by its height against the part is part of the job.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Five kinds of thing are on the table. (1) Magnetic chuck: a fixed steel block 200 mm long (along x), 100 mm wide and 25 mm tall, spanning x 17.0 to 37.0 cm and y -7.0 to +3.0 cm; its flat top is the face. It is made of steel pole pieces separated by three brass lines, 6 mm wide, flush with the face and running across the chuck (along y), centred at x 21.0, 27.0 and 33.0 cm (60 mm apart): the two inner poles are 54 mm wide, wider than the part, the two end poles 37 mm. (2) Rail: a fixed dark steel bar 200 mm long, 10 mm wide and 5 mm tall standing on the face along the chuck's left long edge, from y +2.0 to +3.0 cm, its face toward the middle of the chuck at y +2.0 cm. (3) Part: a loose steel block 40 x 30 x 20 mm, 188 g, coated with blue layout dye, lying on a 40 x 30 mm face on the table centred at x 20.0, y +26.0 cm, its 40 mm length along y. (4) Two low blocking pieces: loose black steel blocks 40 x 18 x 15 mm, 85 g each, lying on a 40 x 18 mm face, length along x, centred at x 25.0, y -25.0 cm and x 17.0, y -31.0 cm. Lying flat they are 15 mm tall, on a side 18 mm: lower than the part either way. (5) Two tall blocking pieces: loose black steel blocks 40 x 24 x 28 mm, 211 g each, lying on a 40 x 24 mm face, length along x, centred at x 17.0, y -25.0 cm and x 25.0, y -31.0 cm: at least 24 mm tall whichever way they lie, taller than the part. All four pieces look alike from above except for their width; only their height says which are lower than the part. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Scored at the end from where the objects rest. 'Face' is the chuck's top. A piece is 'on the chuck' when some of its outline seen from above is over the chuck and its lowest point is at most 21 mm above the face (on the face, on the rail or on something on the chuck). An object is 'held' when it is within 2 mm of a gripper's finger zone: a solid cylinder round the gripper's axis from the finger tips 38 mm back up, flat at the tips, its radius reaching a pad's outer corner at any heading (57 mm fully open; 22 mm closed on a low piece, so a gripper still holding a piece by its middle against an end also holds the part). Score 0 if any blocking piece on the chuck has its top more than 21 mm above the face, however it lies (higher than the 20 mm part: the wheel would strike it). Otherwise four checks, 0.25 each. (R) Against the rail: the part lies on a 40 x 30 mm face, tilted under 3 degrees, its lowest point within 2 mm of the face, wholly over the chuck, its 40 mm length within 5 degrees of the rail's direction, both lower corners of its side facing the rail within 3 mm of the rail's face (and not past it), and it is not held. (B) Across a brass line: a brass line runs under the part with at least 8 mm of the part's length on steel on each side, measured along the rail from the line's edge to the centre of each end face. (E, for each end of the part) Blocked: a blocking piece lies flat on the face (on any of its faces, tilted under 5 degrees, its lowest point within 2 mm of the face) with its top at most 19 mm above the face, is not held, its side facing the part is parallel to the part's end face within 10 degrees, its nearest point is within 3 mm of that end face, and it covers at least 10 mm of the end face's 30 mm depth. B and the two E checks count only when R holds. Score = 0.25 for R, plus 0.25 for B, plus 0.25 for each blocked end. Possible scores: 0; 0.25 (R alone); 0.5 (R and B, or R and one end); 0.75 (R, B and one end, or R and both ends); 1.0 (all four). The trial ends early once 1.0 has held for 1 s with the part and both blocking pieces still (each moved under 2 mm over the last 0.5 s and slower than 5 cm/s); otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. On a step where the grippers cannot be read, nothing counts as held. In a real trial, a top photo and a steel rule give the positions and the brass-line margins, a 3 mm feeler gauge the gaps at the rail and at each end, and a straight edge laid across the part's top shows any piece on the chuck higher than the part.
fidelity: Magnetism is not simulated: the simulator's default friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) holds everything, and the brass lines are flush coloured strips of the chuck. There is no wheel, spindle or table travel. The chuck is a fixed block of full-height pole and brass strips, with coarse poles so a small part can sit on one pole. Every object is a plain uniform box. The scorer reads the grippers' positions and openings, not their heading, so each finger zone is round.
reset_notes: Put the part back on the table centred at x 20.0, y +26.0 cm, its 40 mm length along y and a 40 x 30 mm face down; the low pieces at x 25.0, y -25.0 cm and x 17.0, y -31.0 cm and the tall pieces at x 17.0, y -25.0 cm and x 25.0, y -31.0 cm, each lying on its largest face with its length along x. The chuck and the rail are fixed. Nothing is consumed.
